title: Stop Doing planche lean Wrong: Train Your wrist and shoulder leverage Instead
description: Get into a push-up, lock your arms, and lean forward past your hands. Your planche lean angle is the test of your wrist and shoulder leverage. The technique version: protraction, straight arms, and measuring the lean so it actually grows. Here is how to lean correctly.

scenes.narration: Push-up position. | Top position. | Arms dead straight. | Elbows locked hard. | Now push the floor away | until your upper back | rounds slightly, | shoulder blades spread. | That is protraction. | From there, lean forward | from the ankles, | body one rigid line, | shoulders traveling | past your hands. | Stop at the lean | you can hold | with locked elbows | and a rounded back. | Start your clock. | The clock stops | when an elbow bends, | the back flattens, | or the hips sag. | Note your hand position: | how far past | your shoulders your hands sit | is your angle. | That clean time, | at that angle, | is your number. | Keep both. | The lean is a skill | of position, | and position can be | taught in one session.

scenes.label: AT YOUR MAX CLEAN LEAN IS THE LINE
scenes.sub: under 4 clean sec: position first - 20+: tuck planche path
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Ten clean seconds at your maximum honest lean, elbows locked, back protracted, hips in line, is certified wrist and shoulder leverage. Under four clean seconds, position is your problem before strength is: most first leans fail on setup, not force. Over twenty, the tuck planche stops being a poster on the wall and becomes the next line in your program. This test has two numbers and you must track both. Time tells you endurance at an angle. Hand position tells you the angle itself, and the angle is the skill. A month where your time doubles at the same hand position is a month of surviving. A month where your hands move five centimeters further from your shoulders at the same time is a month of progressing. Train for the second month. Measure both numbers every test, write them as a pair, and let the pair, not your feelings, coach you.

Look at the base. In a normal plank your weight stacks over your hands and the price is small. Leaning moves your center of mass in front of your base, and from that moment your wrists and shoulders are paying for distance. The wrist bends deeper as the lean grows, loading its small bones and connective tissue near end range. The shoulder becomes a straight-arm lever held by the front deltoid and the serratus, the muscle that wraps your shoulder blades forward in protraction. Protraction is not a detail; it is the foundation pour. Without it, the shoulder blades pinch together, the chest sags between the arms, and the lever's top end has nothing solid to push from. With it, the whole front chain becomes one strut from wrist to shoulder to ribs. The lean is priced by distance past the base, and protraction is what lets you afford any distance at all.

Here is the technique truth that saves most leans: the lean happens at the ankles, not the toes, and not the hips. Your body is a rigid plank rotating forward around your feet, shoulders drifting past your hands because the whole plank tilted, not because you walked your hands back or pushed with your toes. Watch two leans from the side. The wrong one is a push-up position that scrunches forward, toes digging, calves working, hips soft. The right one is a statue tipping, silent feet, one line from heels to head. The difference is not strength; both athletes are holding the same plank. It is the direction of the rotation, and it can be corrected with one cue: imagine the floor tilting, and let your whole body ride it forward. Straight-arm tissue adapts slowly, as this season keeps warning, so a lean built on correct rotation compounds for years, while a lean built on scrunches collects wrist pain as its first trophy.

The preparation that makes leans possible is a two-minute wrist ritual, done before every session. Palms flat, fingers forward, rock gently forward until the wrists approach their working angle, ten slow rocks. Fingers turned back, lighter pressure, ten more. Then thirty seconds of lean holds against a wall, wrists at half price. Cold wrists at a max lean is the single most common injury story in planche training, and it is a story with a two-minute prevention chapter. Rituals are not superstition. They are how tissue gets its warning and its warm-up in the same two minutes.

Your advantage is the lean's price list, which is written in your bodyweight. The load past your base is you, so the lighter athlete leans further on identical shoulders, holds it longer, and practices more days per week because his wrists recover overnight. Planche culture quietly knows this: the skill's owners are compact athletes, because the position taxes mass at a punitive rate and rewards relative strength at a generous one. There is a posture dividend too. Protraction and straight-arm tension build the front chain into a shape that reads as powerful at any size: rounded, capped shoulders, dense forearms, a chest held high by its own scaffolding. Presence is structure, and this skill is structure training in its purest form. The mirror cannot weigh you here. It can only watch you lean further than the big guys, on the same floor, with the same gravity.

beats.text: MASS TAXED AT A PUNITIVE RATE

scenes.narration: Lean with me. Protract first, then tip the statue forward to your honest max. Twenty seconds, elbows locked, back rounded. If the elbows soften, tip back and reset. Go.

Here is the fix. Stop leaning before you protract. Set the back first, push the floor away until the shoulder blades spread, and only then tip forward; a lean on a flat, pinched back is a collapse with good marketing. Stop unlocking the elbows to rest mid-hold. The lock is the exercise, so when it goes, the set is over, and resting in a soft-elbow plank trains a different, cheaper skill. Stop moving your hands mid-set to chase distance. Hands are planted at the start, measured, and the lean is earned by rotation, not by walking the base backward. And stop skipping the wrist ritual to save two minutes. Those two minutes are the cheapest insurance in this entire season. The weekly shape: three sessions, wrist ritual, three to five leans at your measured max, every set ending while the lock is still honest. Distance is bought with seconds, and seconds are bought with position.

So, your pair of numbers. Under four clean seconds: position first, and the wrist ritual plus wall leans are your program until the lock feels boring. Four to ten clean at a measured lean: the strut is built and the angle is your frontier. Over ten clean with your hands clearly forward: your wrist and shoulder leverage is certified, and the tuck planche deserves a place in your next month. Retest in thirty days, tape on the floor marking your hand position, because unmeasured leans drift toward optimism. Put your seconds and your hand distance in the comments. Two numbers, one truth. The lean grades your position and your patience, and both respond to training on a schedule of months.
Protract, lock, and tip the statue. That is the planche lean, done right. Subscribe, and bring me your new pair of numbers in thirty days. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
